title: Redo record vocabulary
description:
A typed redo record describes one mutation's file changes as put-file, delete-file, and event-append operations over data-root and worktree paths, with a canonical serialized form.

## Background

Repository publication is driven today by a delta whose four action kinds are `CreateDirectory`, `WriteFile`, `SetMode`, and `DeleteFile`. The redo record is a smaller vocabulary carrying the same intent: the complete new bytes and mode of a written file, a removed path, and an event append expressed as an offset with its bytes. A put creates the parent directories its path needs, so directory creation is implied. A move is a put and a delete in one record, which is what archive execution needs when it copies a document and removes its source.

Paths carry their root class, so one record holds a data-root file, a projection target in the worktree, and a profile asset. The record's home is a scratch directory under the data root. Its name ends in something other than `.tmp`, because the orphan temp sweep matches files by that extension and recurses into subdirectories.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A redo record value holds an ordered set of put-file operations carrying path, bytes, and mode; delete-file operations carrying a path; and at most one event-append operation carrying an offset and its bytes.
- [hard] REQ-02: Record paths are typed by root class, so one record addresses both data-root and worktree targets, and a path outside those roots is rejected at construction.
- [hard] REQ-03: The record round-trips through its serialized form byte-identically, and a record serialized by one process parses in another.
- [hard] REQ-04: Canonical constants name the scratch directory and the record's file name, and the record's name ends in an extension the orphan temp sweep does not match.
- [hard] REQ-05: The module is declared beside the storage layer's other public backends, so its items are reachable from outside the crate and the workspace builds with no warnings while nothing calls them.
- [hard] REQ-06: Round-trip and rejection behaviour are covered by unit tests over the record type.

## Notes

The production module is expected to stay within 250 lines. The storage layer declares its backends publicly, so a module landing before its first caller still builds under the workspace's deny-warnings clippy run.

planning.outcome: A typed record names put-file, delete-file, and event-append operations over rooted paths.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One data type with its serialized form and its path constants.

title: Durable redo record write
description:
The redo record reaches disk synced, with its directory fsynced, before a mutation performs its first live write.

## Background

A redo-only commit protocol has no rollback: once the first live file is replaced there is no way back, so the record is already durable at that moment. The shared atomic-write helper writes a temp file and renames it, with no `sync_all` on the file and no fsync on the parent directory, so it gives reader-visibility atomicity. The one synced write primitive in the tree is the transaction kernel's staging helper, which is retiring.

The helper therefore gains the two operations the record needs: a synced file write and a directory fsync.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Writing a redo record returns after the record's bytes are synced to disk and its containing directory is fsynced.
- [hard] REQ-02: The shared atomic-write module exposes a synced write and a directory fsync as named operations, reached by every caller that needs either.
- [hard] REQ-03: The scratch directory is created when absent, with a mode matching the rest of the data root.
- [hard] REQ-04: A record write that fails partway leaves a residue a later session skips rather than replays.
- [hard] REQ-05: Durability behaviour is covered at the storage unit layer without a wall-clock assertion.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 120 production lines across the record writer and the atomic-write module. Per-file replacement during replay stays on the existing temp-file-and-rename path, whose crash survivability rests on the record.

planning.outcome: The record reaches disk synced with its directory fsynced before any live write.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One synced write path plus two primitives on an existing helper module.

title: File-backend record application
description:
The JSON storage backend applies a redo record to the filesystem and re-applies a leftover one idempotently, stepping through named interruption points.

## Background

Applying a record replaces each put path by temp-file and rename, removes each deleted path, writes the event append at its recorded offset, and removes the record. Re-application is the same code: a put overwrites, a delete tolerates an absent target, and the append rewrites the same bytes at the same offset, so a record applied twice converges on the same state. Parent directories are created as a put needs them, because both backends verify parents and a delta omitting ancestors fails apply.

The positioned append holds three conditions. The offset is the captured file length rather than a line boundary, because the event composer may begin the appended bytes with a separator newline and the torn-tail protocol admits an incomplete final line. The file is opened without append mode, since append mode ignores the offset and would double-append. Re-application truncates to the offset plus the appended length, so a longer file converges.

Interruption points make the mechanism's crash matrix testable at unit cost. They are a closed enum over the steps of apply and re-application, reached through an injector the backend holds, in the shape the storage layer already uses.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Applying a record to a data root replaces each put path, removes each delete path, writes the append at its offset, and removes the record.
- [hard] REQ-02: A put whose parent directories are absent creates them before the replacement.
- [hard] REQ-03: Re-applying a record over a state where some operations already landed produces the same final bytes as a single clean application, for any prefix of the operation order.
- [hard] REQ-04: The event append is written without append mode at the recorded offset, and the file is truncated to the offset plus the appended length.
- [hard] REQ-05: A closed interruption-point enum names each step of apply and re-application, and the backend checks every point through an injector it holds.
- [hard] REQ-06: A record naming a path outside the data root and the worktree is refused before any live write.
- [hard] REQ-07: The apply module is declared beside the storage layer's other public backends, so the workspace builds with no warnings while nothing calls it.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 350 production lines. The interruption points name the steps of this mechanism alone.

planning.outcome: The JSON backend applies a record idempotently through named interruption points.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One apply routine over a vocabulary of three operations, with its interruption points.

title: Memory-backend record application
description:
The in-memory storage backend holds a redo record as a value and applies it by stepping through the same interruption points as the filesystem backend.

## Background

The in-memory backend exists so command workflows are testable without a filesystem, and the project requires one behavioural contract across both backends. The in-memory session mirrors the filesystem kernel today by walking the same failure points in the same order over an in-memory residue, with one deliberately skipped step marked so the point set stays identical across backends.

The redo record keeps that shape and shrinks it. The in-memory backend stores the record as a value beside its state map, applies its operations to that map in the same order, and checks the same interruption points, so a crash injected at a given point means the same thing on both backends. The residue carries the record alone.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A mutation on the in-memory backend installs a redo record as a value before it changes any state entry.
- [hard] REQ-02: Applying the record updates put entries, removes delete entries, and extends the event entry at its recorded offset.
- [hard] REQ-03: Re-applying a leftover record over a backend that already holds part of it leaves the backend in the same semantic state as a clean application.
- [hard] REQ-04: The backend checks the same interruption-point values, in the same order, as the filesystem backend, and each point is reachable on both.
- [hard] REQ-05: The in-memory residue carries the record and nothing else.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 200 production lines, against roughly 340 lines of kernel modelling this replaces.

planning.outcome: The in-memory backend holds a record as a value and steps the same interruption points.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One value-held record applied to an existing state map over the same point enum.

title: Write-set and event-log conflict check
description:
A mutation compares the live bytes of the files it writes, and the event log's length and tail, with what it read, returning a retryable conflict on any difference.

## Background

The current check re-captures the mutation's entire read set immediately before publication and compares the whole image, costing a full reread of every registry, the event log, and every issue file. The replacement is scoped to the files the mutation writes, with the event log compared as its length together with its last four kilobytes.

The tail window is defined in bytes because the torn-tail protocol admits an incomplete final line in the log. The check reads: the live file's length equals the captured length, and the live last `min(len, 4096)` bytes equal the captured ones. The event log is excluded from the byte-for-byte write-set comparison so one path has one answer; until the append encoding lands, the log is a put path whose whole contents would otherwise be reread.

The accepted cost is that an external edit to a file a mutation read but does not write goes undetected during that mutation, making one result stale. The repository write lock keeps concurrent jit writers of repository state out of the window.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Before a record is written, the live bytes of every put and delete path other than the event log are compared with the bytes the mutation read, and a difference yields a retryable conflict that changes nothing.
- [hard] REQ-02: The event log's live length and its last `min(len, 4096)` bytes are compared with the captured ones, and a difference yields the same retryable conflict.
- [hard] REQ-03: A file the mutation read but does not write is left out of the comparison, and its change leaves the mutation admissible.
- [hard] REQ-04: The conflict names the path that moved.
- [hard] REQ-05: A target the mutation expected absent passes the check when absent and refuses it when occupied.
- [hard] REQ-06: Conflict and success behaviour are covered at the storage unit layer, including an empty log and a log shorter than the tail window.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 150 production lines. The comparison runs under the repository write lock the session already holds.

planning.outcome: A moved write target or event-log tail yields a retryable conflict before anything changes.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One comparison over a bounded set of paths plus one length-and-tail check.

title: Shared interruption conformance suite
description:
One conformance suite proves the redo record's interruption matrix on both storage backends, compile-enforced over the interruption-point enum.

## Background

The record's crash contract is that an interruption at any step leaves the complete old state, or the complete new state once the leftover record is applied again. That is the mechanism's own behaviour matrix, so it is proven once, against the mechanism, and each consumer proves only that it reaches the mechanism.

Both backends run the same suite, driven by generic functions over the storage trait, the pattern the storage suite already uses. Coverage is compile-enforced over the point enum: adding a point without classifying it fails the build. The list it replaces is hand-maintained and covers thirty of thirty-six points.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One suite drives an interruption at each interruption-point value, on the filesystem backend and the in-memory backend, from the same driver.
- [hard] REQ-02: After an interruption before the record is durable, the repository reads back as the complete old state.
- [hard] REQ-03: After an interruption at or after the record becomes durable, re-applying the leftover record yields the complete new state, and applying it a second time yields it again.
- [hard] REQ-04: Coverage over the point enum is compile-enforced, so a new point fails the build until it is classified.
- [hard] REQ-05: The suite asserts semantic state rather than a copied byte inventory, and each test states one property.
- [hard] REQ-06: The suite adds no new integration-test target.

## Notes

Expected footprint is under 400 test lines. The suite lives beside the mechanism in the storage layer, the cheapest layer that can observe the property. Session-open replay is a separate property with its own owner.

planning.outcome: One suite proves the record's interruption matrix on both backends, compile-enforced.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One driver over an existing point enum, run twice against two backends.

title: Consumer-side publication matrix retirement
description:
Each publication consumer keeps one test that it goes through the shared publication mechanism, in place of a copy of the mechanism's crash matrix.

## Background

The project requires a mechanism's behaviour matrix to be proven once against the mechanism, with each consumer proving only that it reaches it. Publication violates that in four places. A profile-lifecycle suite drives the whole failure-point set through `profile apply` and classifies it with a compile-enforced thirty-six-arm match. A gate-durability test, two linked-checkout write-policy tests, and two recover-command tests each re-inject a commit-decision or prepared-state failure to restate the same convergence property.

The record's own conformance suite already owns the matrix and restores compile-enforced coverage of the point set, so the consumer copies have an owner to defer to. This is also the largest single-file reduction available outside the kernel.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The profile-lifecycle interruption suite no longer enumerates a publication failure-point set, and `profile apply` retains one test asserting that it publishes through the shared session.
- [hard] REQ-02: Gate evaluation retains one test asserting that a gate run's durable evidence is coupled to the issue change.
- [hard] REQ-03: The linked-checkout write-policy suite retains its policy coverage, with publication convergence left to the mechanism's suite.
- [hard] REQ-04: The recover command's suite retains its command-contract tests, with journal-shaped prepared state left out.
- [hard] REQ-05: No exhaustive classification of a publication failure-point set survives outside the mechanism's own suite.
- [hard] REQ-06: The change removes more test lines than it adds.

## Notes

Stale-capture rejection under concurrent profile application is a separate property with its own suite and survives untouched here.

planning.outcome: Each publication consumer keeps one test that it reaches the shared mechanism.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Four known suites shed a matrix another suite owns, with no production change.

title: Superseded rollback coverage retirement
description:
The storage session suite sheds the coverage of rollback reachability, journal records, verified backups, worktree companions, and kernel-point convergence, each property having an owner against the redo record or none at all.

## Background

Publication converges today by rolling a partially published change back through verified synced backups, and its suite proves that: reverse-action edges, rollback decisions, backup restoration, companion control directories, and stage cleanup. The redo record keeps coupled-state convergence and the concurrent-writer check, and drops rollback reachability deliberately. A half-applied record is finished forward.

Two further tests state interruption convergence over the kernel's thirty-six-variant enum: one boundary test and one that runs one hundred and eighty convergence checks in a single test. The record's conformance suite owns that property now, against the record's own points, so the kernel-enum copies go with the rest. What the session suite keeps is cross-backend byte parity and finalizer determinism, which are independent of the commit mechanism.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The storage session suite retains no test whose assertion is that a partially published change is reversed.
- [hard] REQ-02: The suite retains no test asserting journal contents, backup restoration, companion control directories, or staged-then-reversed publication.
- [hard] REQ-03: The suite retains no interruption-convergence test driven by the kernel's failure-point set, and no hand-maintained list of those points.
- [hard] REQ-04: Cross-backend byte-parity coverage and finalizer-determinism coverage survive unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-05: The suite compiles and passes against the current publication mechanism after the change.
- [hard] REQ-06: The change removes more test lines than it adds.

## Notes

The kernel module's own test module exercises the kernel directly and retires with the module it covers.

planning.outcome: The session suite keeps byte parity and finalizer determinism, shedding rollback coverage.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One suite sheds the half whose guarantee the charter decision supersedes.

title: Publication failure injection repoint
description:
A publication-failure injection in the workspace names an interruption point the redo record defines.

## Background

Publication-failure injection reaches nine command and test modules outside the storage layer: profile, gate, issue, bulk update, dependency, init, gate check, the shared command module, and the concurrent-profile-application suite. Each names a variant of the kernel's thirty-six-point enum. Once the session commits through the record, those points are never reached, and once the kernel retires they no longer compile.

Repointing them ahead of the commit swap keeps each later step compiling and passing. The concurrent-profile-application suite is ported rather than retired: it owns stale-capture rejection under contention, a property the redo record has too, and it is the only test of it.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Each publication-failure injection in the workspace names an interruption point the record defines.
- [hard] REQ-02: The kernel's failure-point enum is referenced only by the kernel and by the storage modules that still host it.
- [hard] REQ-03: The concurrent-profile-application suite injects a record interruption point and still asserts that a contender never publishes a stale capture.
- [hard] REQ-04: Command-layer test helpers expose the record's points, with the kernel's points removed from their surface.
- [hard] REQ-05: The workspace builds with no warnings and the suite passes with no test held out of the default run.

## Notes

The record's points exist at this stage while the kernel still commits, so an injection repointed here fires once the session commits through the record.

planning.outcome: A publication-failure injection names an interruption point the record defines.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Nine known modules swap one injector vocabulary for another.

title: Session open applies a leftover record
description:
Opening a mutation session applies a leftover redo record idempotently on both backends and reports how many records it applied.

## Background

Session open runs crash recovery today: it lists pending transactions in two control locations, validates each journal, and either rolls a prepared transaction back or completes a committed one forward. Under the redo record that becomes one step: read a leftover record from the data root's scratch directory and apply it, which is idempotent, then remove it.

This lands while the kernel still commits. With no writer of records yet, the new path is a no-op on a live repository and is exercised by seeding a record directly, which is what makes it safe to separate from the commit swap.

The dispatch's reported count feeds the recover command's output and the server's startup report, so its meaning changes from recovered transactions to applied records.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Opening a session on either backend applies a leftover redo record before any capture, and removes it.
- [hard] REQ-02: Opening a session twice over the same seeded record leaves the repository in the same semantic state as opening it once.
- [hard] REQ-03: The dispatch report counts applied redo records, and its count reaches the recover command and the server's startup report.
- [hard] REQ-04: A session opened on a repository with no leftover record performs no extra read beyond checking the scratch directory.
- [hard] REQ-05: A malformed leftover record yields a typed recovery failure naming the record, leaving the repository unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-06: Journal recovery still runs at session open while the kernel commits, so a repository left by the kernel converges as it does today.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 200 production lines.

planning.outcome: Opening a session applies a leftover redo record on both backends.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One dispatch body gains a record check beside the recovery it will replace.

title: Session commit through the redo record
description:
A mutation's apply commits through one redo record in place of the journaled kernel, with the whole-read-set re-capture gone.

## Background

Every repository publisher in the workspace converges on one seam: the mutation session's apply. Issue commands, dependency edits, template application, validation repair, profile lifecycle, configuration edits, archive execution, gate runs, project rendering, and document commands all reach the kernel through it. That makes the seam the place to change the commit mechanism with no publisher touched.

Apply's shape becomes: derive the record from the delta the plan carries, compare the live bytes of the files it writes and the event log's length and tail, write the record durably, apply it, and remove it. The re-capture of the whole read set and its whole-image comparison, which ran immediately before journal preparation on both backends, is gone.

Machine-local control files stay outside the record and outside the lock: worktree identity, the server pid file, the server log, and claims under the version-control directory.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The mutation session's apply builds a redo record from the plan's delta, writes it durably, applies it, and removes it, on the filesystem backend and the in-memory backend.
- [hard] REQ-02: Publishers reach publication through the same session trait they used before, with their call sites unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-03: Apply's only pre-commit check is over the files it writes and the event log's length and tail; the read-set re-capture and whole-image comparison are gone from both backends.
- [hard] REQ-04: A repository left by an interruption converges on the complete old state, or on the complete new state once the next session opens.
- [hard] REQ-05: Worktree identity, the server pid file, the server log, and claim state are carried outside the record and outside the repository write lock.
- [hard] REQ-06: The session trait's shape is unchanged, so both out-of-crate re-implementations of it compile unmodified.
- [hard] REQ-07: A delta that creates an absent data root still reaches the transaction kernel, so the kernel keeps a caller and the workspace builds with no warnings.
- [hard] REQ-08: The interruption point that named the read-set revalidation leaves the failure-point enum with the revalidation itself, so no point survives that nothing constructs.
- [hard] REQ-09: The suite passes with no test held out of the default run.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 300 production lines, against the in-memory kernel modelling of roughly 340 lines it replaces. The transaction kernel's one remaining caller after this change is the creation of an absent data root, which apply already distinguishes by the delta's root class. Keeping that branch is what leaves the kernel referenced until initialization takes over.

The read-set revalidation is the only interruption point in the failure-point enum with no site inside the kernel. Its two constructors are the revalidation blocks this task removes, and the test-side constructors are gone by the time it runs, so the variant would be left never constructed in a crate-private enum. It leaves with the code it named.

planning.outcome: A mutation's apply commits through one redo record with no re-capture of its read set.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One apply body swaps its commit mechanism beneath an unchanged trait.

title: Init publisher for an absent data root
description:
Repository initialization creates an absent data root through a small publisher of its own: a synced sibling stage directory published by a no-replace rename.

## Background

Initialization has no publication code of its own. It builds a plan and hands it to the shared mutation session, and the kernel is what allocates a stage directory beside the data root, stages every file with create-new and sync, re-verifies each staged file against a recorded identity, rebinds the parent, and publishes the root with a no-replace rename. An external journal makes an interrupted initialization recoverable.

The redo record cannot do this: its home is a scratch directory under a data root that does not exist yet. Initialization therefore keeps the creation protocol and sheds the journal around it: write the new root into a sibling stage directory, sync it, publish it with a no-replace rename, and report an occupied-root error when the destination is taken. An orphan stage left by an interrupted run is removed by the next initialization.

Worktree files that initialization writes, such as the version-control attributes file, publish through the redo record like any other worktree target.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Initializing an absent data root writes the complete scaffold into a sibling stage directory, syncs it, and publishes it with a no-replace rename.
- [hard] REQ-02: An occupied destination yields an occupied-data-root error and leaves the existing root untouched.
- [hard] REQ-03: An interruption before the rename leaves no data root, and the next initialization removes the stage directory it left.
- [hard] REQ-04: Worktree files the initialization writes publish through the redo record, in the same session.
- [hard] REQ-05: The publisher carries the creation protocol alone: no journal, no external bootstrap control directory, no post-publication identity re-verification.
- [hard] REQ-06: Initialization reaches the transaction kernel nowhere.
- [hard] REQ-07: Each kernel item left without a caller carries a dead-code allowance at the narrowest scope covering it, written with the removal condition "removed when the transaction kernel retires", and the workspace builds with no warnings.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 250 production lines in a module of its own. This is the one publication path beside the redo record, and it exists because no scratch directory precedes the root it creates.

This removes the kernel's last publication caller. Its four storage modules keep callers, because session open still runs journal recovery: the recovery dispatch names the kernel type, the control-location enum, and the staging helpers until the kernel retires. What loses its last caller is the publication half inside the kernel module — the delta executor and the private graph it drives, together with the outcome struct's hash field, whose only reader is the apply path this task leaves. Those items are crate-private, so the compiler's dead-code lint reports them under the workspace's deny-warnings build, and the allowance is the named, versioned boundary that carries them to the task that removes them.

planning.outcome: A fresh data root appears whole through a synced stage directory and a no-replace rename.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One creation protocol moves into a module of its own with the journal shed.

title: Data-root ignore file as a derived materialization
description:
The data root's ignore file naming the scratch directory is composed from the repository's own declarations, so initialization and derived-state repair both produce it.

## Background

The commit point lives in a scratch directory under the data root. Keeping that directory out of version control is a correctness property: a committed record would be applied on a checkout that never performed the mutation, and a merge would collide over it.

No shipped code writes an ignore entry. This repository ignores the directory through a hand-maintained entry in its root ignore file, which an adopter running initialization does not get, and which an existing repository would need a migration to gain.

A derived materialization answers both. The default ruleset and the default schemas are composed from what the repository declares and emitted by one producer that initialization and derived-state repair both reach, so an existing repository converges on the correct content at its next repair rather than through a migration path. The data root's ignore file joins that family. The worktree attributes file is the precedent for the engine owning a version-control control file: a declared well-known path with an ownership identity and a typed claim outcome.

The composer is independent of how a mutation commits: the ignore file is one more data-root action in the plan initialization already publishes. It lands before the first record is written under the scratch directory, so no repository holds a commit point the engine has not asked version control to ignore.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: One composer emits the data root's ignore file from the repository's declarations, naming the scratch directory, and both initialization and derived-state repair reach it.
- [hard] REQ-02: Running derived-state repair on a repository whose data root lacks the file produces it, and running it again produces no action.
- [hard] REQ-03: An ignore file carrying authored lines beside the engine's keeps those lines, with the engine's ownership boundary proven before any write.
- [hard] REQ-04: The adopter's root ignore file is left unread and unwritten.
- [hard] REQ-05: This repository's data root carries the composed ignore file, and the hand-maintained scratch-directory entry in its root ignore file is gone.
- [hard] REQ-06: A repository initialized fresh reports no untracked scratch content in its version-control status after a mutation.
- [hard] REQ-07: The file is composed through the publication in use when this lands, with no dependency on how a mutation commits.

## Notes

Expected additive footprint is under 120 production lines. The composer emits nothing when the target sits outside the captured closure, which is how the neighbouring default-ruleset producer stays ownership-safe.

planning.outcome: The data root's ignore file is composed from the repository's own declarations.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One composer beside the default-ruleset producer both entry points already reach.

title: Security review scope names live mechanisms
description:
The security-review gate's declared scope names the mechanisms the repository has.

## Background

The gate registry declares each gate's review scope, and the security-review entry lists the areas a reviewer is expected to cover: path containment, symlink and junction races, recovery journals, untrusted manifest content, and the rest. Recovery journals stop existing when the transaction kernel retires, so the scope names an area with no code behind it and a reviewer is directed at nothing.

The registry is the authority and the rules-and-gates reference is its projection, so the line is corrected at source and the projection is re-rendered.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The security-review gate's declared scope names no recovery journal, and it names the redo record's publication and replay in its place.
- [hard] REQ-02: The remaining scope areas are unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-03: The rules-and-gates reference matches the registry, produced by rendering rather than by hand.
- [hard] REQ-04: Repository validation passes against the edited registry.

planning.outcome: The security-review scope names the mechanisms the repository has.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One declared scope line corrected at source with its projection re-rendered.

title: Re-homed no-follow file open
description:
The no-follow regular-file open lives outside the transaction kernel module, where its readers already are.

## Background

The kernel module exports one helper with consumers outside the transaction path: a capability-relative open that refuses symbolic links and non-regular files. Six call sites use it, five in the JSON storage backend, including the event-log read path, and one in artifact planning. It is the only kernel export that survives the kernel.

Moving it first keeps the kernel's retirement a pure removal.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The no-follow regular-file open lives in a storage module other than the transaction kernel, with its refusal of symbolic links and non-regular targets unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-02: Every current call site reaches it at its new home, and it exists in one copy.
- [hard] REQ-03: Its error type is independent of the transaction kernel's error enum.
- [hard] REQ-04: Refusal of a symbolic link and of a directory is covered at the storage unit layer.

planning.outcome: The no-follow regular-file open lives outside the transaction kernel module.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One function moves between modules with its six call sites updated.

title: Transaction kernel retirement
description:
The journaled transaction kernel, its journal, its staging module, its recovery arms, and its control-plane module leave the storage layer, and recovery discovery keys on the redo record.

## Background

With the mutation session committing through the redo record and initialization publishing an absent root through its own module, the kernel has no caller. What goes with it is named precisely, because several of the constructs are known by descriptions rather than by their own names.

The rollback kernel is `FileTransactionKernel` with `rollback_repository_actions` and `rollback_repository_action`. Transaction backup is `prepare_repository_backup`, `restore_verified_backup`, `remove_redundant_backup`, `backup_authority`, the backups control subdirectory, and the journal's backup fields. The staging directory is the `transaction_staging` module, `stage_authority`, `prepare_staged_data_action`, `create_directory_stage_name`, the stages control subdirectory, and the journal's stage fields. Reverse actions are the two reverse-action failure-point variants and the rollback functions they bracket. The worktree companion is the companion marker constant, `CompanionDirs`, the four companion control functions, the orphan-companion sweep, and the companion-need field. With them go the journal module, the journal-shaped half of the recovery module including its thirty-six-variant failure-point enum and its injector plumbing, and the control-plane module, which has no production caller.

Recovery discovery is production behaviour: it recognizes a repository needing recovery by an external bootstrap protocol marker or an internal transactions subdirectory. Under the record the marker is a record file directly under the data root's scratch directory, so a repository whose index is absent still reaches recovery.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: No rollback kernel, reverse-action path, verified backup, staging directory, or worktree companion survives in the workspace under any spelling.
- [hard] REQ-02: The transaction journal module, the journal-shaped recovery module, the staging module, and the control-plane module are gone, along with the failure-point enum and the injector plumbing that served them.
- [hard] REQ-03: Both storage backends carry no modelling of the journaled kernel's phases.
- [hard] REQ-04: Redo-record publication and the initialization root publisher are the two paths that write repository state, the second reached only for an absent data root.
- [hard] REQ-05: Recovery discovery recognizes a pending redo record under the data root's scratch directory, and recognizes no journal location.
- [hard] REQ-06: No dead-code allowance introduced for the kernel's unreferenced interval survives in the workspace.
- [hard] REQ-07: The workspace builds with no warnings and the suite passes with no test held out of the default run.
- [hard] REQ-08: The change removes more lines than it adds, across production code and tests.

## Notes

The kernel module's own test module retires with the module it covers. The lock-order guard module stays: it enforces acquisition order rather than durability, and its property survives.

planning.outcome: The journaled kernel with its journal, staging, recovery, and control plane leaves storage.

title: Single-pass mutation capture
description:
A mutation reads the repository once instead of in three gated rounds, and the phase-to-phase coherence check goes with the phasing.

## Background

A changing mutation performs six capture rounds: two in a preflight session, three in the attempt session, and one at apply. The attempt rounds are an ad-hoc protocol in the command layer: a registry-only round, a round adding the event log and every indexed issue file, and a third re-reading all of it plus per-profile records, working-tree document paths, precheck prompts, and gate-run paths. An overlap-stability check gates each round against the one before it.

With publication comparing only the files it writes, the phasing has nothing left to certify. A mutation reads its base set in one pass, and a caller's named paths and listings join that same round. The apply-time round is already gone, and the preflight collapses to one round.

The first cut keeps reading every indexed issue, because dependency-graph derivation and hierarchy validation need the full issue set to detect cycles and transitive redundancy. That cost scales with issue count, which is what the latency target requires.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A changing mutation performs one capture round in its attempt and one in its preflight, with no round gated by an overlap-stability check.
- [hard] REQ-02: No phase-one capture specification, phase-three specification, or overlap-stability check survives in the workspace.
- [hard] REQ-03: The capture's base specification reads the registries, the index, the event log, the indexed issue files, and the plan documents a transition rule consults; a caller's named paths and listings are added to that one round.
- [hard] REQ-04: Gate-run result capture joins the same round, with its own further rounds gone.
- [hard] REQ-05: A pure producer reading a path the capture did not discover still fails typed.
- [hard] REQ-06: Capture remains budget-bounded, with no whole-worktree recursion.
- [hard] REQ-07: The change removes more lines than it adds.

## Notes

The phase-two closure-change retry test loses its referent and goes with the phasing; the property that a changed closure discards and recaptures survives as a single-pass recapture.

planning.outcome: A mutation reads the repository once rather than in three gated rounds.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One capture routine collapses from three rounds to one behind unchanged entry points.

title: Listing fingerprint retirement
description:
A captured listing carries child names without per-child identity, so a mutation stops hashing directory entries it does not write.

## Background

A captured image carries, beside its file entries, a fingerprint of each discovered directory listing: the complete set of child names with their identities. Its purpose was to detect a sibling file appearing or vanishing between capture and commit. Archive planning and the shared command module read those listings as data — which children exist, under which directory — at nine sites, so name discovery stays; the per-child identity is what goes.

The race-detection guarantee is dropped deliberately. A mutation no longer detects a directory-entry race, and the repository write lock is what makes that acceptable for the files a mutation writes.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: No listing fingerprint type and no fingerprint accessor survives in the workspace, and a captured listing carries child names without per-child identity.
- [hard] REQ-02: Commands that consulted a listing as data still read the child names they need from the captured image.
- [hard] REQ-03: Capture byte and name budgets still bound what a listing read may consume, and a rogue directory still refuses the capture.
- [hard] REQ-04: The source-text policy assertion naming the fingerprint accessor is retargeted, with its reason stated where it lands.
- [hard] REQ-05: The change removes more lines than it adds.

## Notes

The budget coverage over oversized listings states a real property and survives.

planning.outcome: Repository images carry child names without listing fingerprints.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One per-child identity leaves an existing capture structure across known call sites.

footprint.uncertainty: The fingerprint accessor is reached from seventeen files at thirty-two sites (investigation section 3.2); the listed files are the heaviest.

title: Transaction fields leave the command output
description:
The profile and recover commands report the redo record: no plan hash, transaction identifier, or cleanup-pending flag, and a count of applied records, in one cutover across output, schema, bridge, and reference.

## Background

Four output surfaces name the mechanism being replaced. The plan hash is a digest over every captured entry, documented in the profile apply and upgrade output. The transaction identifier names a journal directory. The cleanup-pending flag warns that a control directory survived. The recover command emits a `transactions_recovered` key and a matching human line, fed by the session-open dispatch's count.

None has a referent under the redo record. A superseded representation is removed at cutover rather than re-derived under a new name, so no replacement identifier appears in place of the three profile fields; the recover count survives with the name of what it now counts.

The bridge that generates tool definitions from the command schema and the adopter reference both carry the fields. The release notes record the change, because it is adopter-visible.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-02: The command schema declares none of the three fields, and the generated bridge tool definitions match the schema.

- [hard] REQ-04: No replacement identifier appears in place of the three fields.
- [hard] REQ-05: The recover command's machine-readable output and its rendered line name applied redo records, with the same meaning in both, and both adopter pages documenting the command agree on the name.

Its purpose was to let publication revalidate that the image it publishes from is the one the planner derived from. The redo record compares the bytes of the files it writes, so the digest has no consumer.

The profile output field it fed has already gone, and the journal with it.

title: Publication path source guards

Source guards fail when a second repository publication path appears, retargeted from the kernel they name today.

## Background

A scratch-built suite carries source-text guards over the workspace: no raw filesystem writes in the command layer, no predecessor or compatibility module, one canonical renderer owner, one package-tree publisher, and a capture that addresses no source by pathname. Its header names the kernel module as the compiler-enforced half of the guarantee, and several guards name the kernel and the atomic-write module directly.

With the kernel gone, the guards retarget onto what carries the property: the redo record is the one mechanism that writes repository state, and the initialization root publisher is its single named exception.

title: Positioned event-log append
description:
The finalizer emits the event-log change as an offset with its bytes, so publication writes the appended lines in place.

## Background

Every mutation rewrites the event log as a whole-file replacement: the composer reads the captured prefix, composes prefix plus new lines, and emits one whole-file write. The log is several megabytes and grows with project history, so the cost of a mutation grows with it. The action vocabulary has no append operation, and the log has one writer, which makes this a contained change.

The offset is the captured file length rather than a line boundary. The composer inserts one separator newline when a non-empty prefix lacks one, so the appended bytes may begin with a newline. Torn-tail certification is preserved: a prefix not ending in a newline whose final line is invalid JSON still refuses non-certifying events, and the lifecycle certifier is still the line immediately following the torn partial, which under this encoding is the first line of the appended bytes.

Readers are unaffected: the log is read whole under a shared lock, which is equally correct over an in-place append.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A mutation's record carries the event-log change as an offset with the appended bytes.
- [hard] REQ-02: The offset is the captured file length, and appended bytes beginning with a separator newline are preserved verbatim.
- [hard] REQ-03: Torn-tail certification behaves as it does today: an uncertified torn tail refuses non-certifying events, and the certifier is the first appended line.
- [hard] REQ-04: The appended bytes are the only log bytes a mutation writes.
- [hard] REQ-05: Reading the log after a positioned append yields the same parsed events as reading it after a whole-file composition of the same content.
- [hard] REQ-06: The adopter pages stating how the event log grows describe a positioned append at the captured length.
- [hard] REQ-07: The change adds under 150 production lines.

## Notes

The delta's action vocabulary is matched exhaustively at six sites, four of them inside the kernel module, so this encoding lands once that module is gone.

planning.outcome: The finalizer emits the event-log change as an offset with its bytes.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One composer emits an offset instead of whole contents, preserving torn-tail behaviour.

title: Benchmark harness event-log scale
description:
The benchmark harness measures a label update on a repository whose event log is ten times larger, with the issue set unchanged.

## Background

The harness clones two repositories onto a scratch filesystem, syncs the live data root in, and takes the median of three runs for three scenarios: a changing label update, an idempotent one, and one refused for a missing lease. It measures wall clock.

Isolating the event-log term needs a fourth fixture: the same repository, the same issues, the same index, and a log ten times the bytes. The honest construction replays real event lines with fresh identifiers, because every line must parse and the log's merge behaviour assumes one record per identifier. Inflating the log during the sync step keeps the fixture a real data root that goes through the same capture and publication as the unmodified one.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The harness produces a fixture whose event log is at least ten times the source repository's log in bytes, with the same issue set and the same index.
- [hard] REQ-02: Every line in the inflated log parses, and event identifiers stay unique.
- [hard] REQ-03: The harness runs the changing, idempotent, and lease-refused scenarios against the inflated fixture and reports each median beside the unmodified one.
- [hard] REQ-04: The harness reports the byte size of each log it compared.
- [hard] REQ-05: The harness states the absolute paths it depends on and fails with a message naming a missing one.

planning.outcome: The harness measures a label update against a ten-times larger event log.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One fixture construction step added to an existing script with one extra scenario group.

title: Publication cost evidence
description:
A committed artifact reports label-update latency before and after the change, on both repositories and on a ten-times larger event log, together with the workspace line balance.

## Background

Performance is protected by benchmark evidence rather than by a timing assertion in the suite. A wall-clock assertion would be the workspace's first throughput assertion, contradicts the project's position that elapsed time is the wrong thing to decide a test on, and could not be parked when it flaked.

The artifact is produced by the repository's benchmark harness against two builds: the base revision and the tip. It reports a changing label update, an idempotent one, and a lease-refused one, on the adopter-scale repository and on this repository, plus the ten-times log fixture. It also records the cumulative line balance of the work over the workspace's Rust sources from the base revision.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A committed artifact reports the median of three runs for a changing, an idempotent, and a lease-refused label update, before and after, on the adopter-scale repository and on this repository.
- [hard] REQ-02: The median wall time of a changing label update after the change is under 100 milliseconds on both repositories.
- [hard] REQ-03: The artifact reports the same scenarios on the ten-times event-log fixture, and the changing-update median differs from the unmodified repository's by less than ten percent.
- [hard] REQ-04: The artifact states the event-log byte size and the issue count of each repository it measured.
- [hard] REQ-05: The artifact reports the cumulative Rust line balance from the base revision `34d37f8be` over the workspace, measured with `git diff --shortstat 34d37f8be -- '*.rs'`, and that balance removes more lines than it adds.
- [hard] REQ-06: The artifact names the harness, the two builds, and the machine conditions that produced it.

## Notes

The base revision is Rust-identical to the revision at which this work began, so either spelling measures the same thing.

planning.outcome: A committed artifact reports label-update latency before and after plus the line balance.

title: Repository declarations state the redo record
description:
The invariant registry states publication as it now works, and the charter decision on profile publication matches it.

## Background

Two project invariants describe the superseded mechanism. The atomic-writes statement names temp-file and rename for replacements and verified staging with no-replace publication for new files; a positioned append and a record applied at session open fall outside it. The derived-state-coherence statement requires a mutation to derive from one final repository view, which a single-pass capture followed by a write-scoped comparison no longer certifies.

Both are rewritten. The rewritten atomic-writes statement carries four things: file replacement by temp-file and rename, event-log growth by positioned append, the synced redo record as the commit point with idempotent application at session open, and repository initialization's synced stage with a no-replace rename for an absent root.

The registry is the sole authority. The agent-guidance projection is generated from it. A third copy of each statement ships by hand in this repository's own profile package and diverges silently unless it moves with the registry. The charter's profile-lifecycle decision says a profile publishes through one recoverable transaction; the charter is the projection source for the generated decision region, so it is edited at source and re-rendered.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The atomic-writes statement names file replacement by temp-file and rename, event-log growth by positioned append, the synced redo record as the commit point with idempotent application at session open, and initialization's synced stage with a no-replace rename for an absent root, and it scopes no-replace publication to repository content rather than to the engine's own control state.
- [hard] REQ-02: The derived-state-coherence statement describes the view a mutation derives from as it now is, and states publication recoverability in terms of the redo record.
- [hard] REQ-03: The generated agent-guidance projection matches the registry, produced by rendering.
- [hard] REQ-04: The shipped profile package's copies of both statements match the registry.
- [hard] REQ-05: The charter's profile-lifecycle decision describes publication through one redo record, edited at source, and the generated decision region is re-rendered.
- [hard] REQ-06: Generated regions carry only rendered content.

planning.outcome: The invariant registry and the charter decision name the record.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Two registry statements with one charter entry, rendered through declared projections.

title: Storage format reference states the redo record
description:
The storage-format reference names the scratch directory as the commit point's home, describes publication as a redo record, and describes recovery as application at session open.

## Background

The reference is the canonical adopter statement of the repository layout and its write contract. It lists the data root's contents without the scratch directory, states that pending recoverable multi-file transactions live under a transactions subdirectory, names an external bootstrap control directory, and calls the whole thing a transaction, rollback, and mandatory-recovery contract. It also states the machine-local set kept out of version control, where the scratch directory's ignore entry belongs.

The guarantees page is the epicentre in the adopter-facing concepts family. title: Command and recovery references state the redo record

title: Generated storage-records reference matches the append encoding
description:
The generated storage-records reference is regenerated from its Rust source and describes the event log's positioned append.

## Background

The storage-records reference is generated from the record definitions the binary writes with, and its generator's own header states that its event-log sample lines are encoded the way the repository-state finalizer publishes them. The finalizer's encoding changes when the log starts growing by positioned append, so the generator and the page move with it.

Regenerating after the source prose changes is what keeps the page honest; editing generated output would edit a projection rather than its authority.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The generated reference is produced by regeneration from its source.
- [hard] REQ-02: The storage-records reference and its generator describe the event log's positioned append.
- [hard] REQ-03: Regenerating a second time produces no diff.

planning.outcome: The generated storage-records reference matches the append encoding.

title: Architecture materialization note rewrite
description:
The materialization architecture note describes record publication in place of the sections describing the kernel, its journal, and its recovery.

## Background

The note is the contributor-facing description of repository-state materialization. It is accurate today and obsolete the moment the mechanism changes: it names the kernel, the journal, and the recovery module in its layer map and its diagrams, describes the two-phase capture specification and its budgets, describes the expected-preimage check and the plan hash, describes the mutation-session contract down to composing the exact event-log content, and carries a session-open recovery section with an apply-time re-capture and a sequence diagram. Its closing pointer sends a new contributor to three files that will not exist.

The note is in the repository's permanent documentation set, so it is maintained. The archived copies under the archive root are pinned.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The layer map, the pipeline description, and the diagrams name the redo record and its application at session open.
- [hard] REQ-02: The capture description states one read pass with its budgets, and names no capture phase or overlap-stability check.
- [hard] REQ-03: The commit description states the write-scoped comparison, the synced record, the apply order, and idempotent re-application.
- [hard] REQ-04: The closing reading order points at files that exist after the change.
- [hard] REQ-05: The pure-producer and repair-derivation sections are preserved where they remain accurate.
- [hard] REQ-06: The core-system-design note and the architecture-pitfalls study state the same mechanism.

## Notes

Archived work products are pinned to the revision that produced them and stay as they are.

planning.outcome: The materialization architecture note describes record publication.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One maintained note whose obsolete sections the investigation enumerates by line span.

title: Testing guide publication-cost evidence
description:
The testing guide names the redo-record benchmark harness as its publication-cost evidence, and the journal-shaped harness it replaces stops shipping.

## Background

The guide pins publication-cost numbers to an artifact produced by a nine-hundred-line script written around the journal's shape: it asserts the presence and absence of an external bootstrap control directory and counts directory fsync calls, a property of the journal's phase barriers. Both the numbers and the named evidence contract go stale on the first day of the change.

The guide also maintains a per-test cost attribution table naming tests that this work retires or renames, and a build-budget note derived from measured worst-case figures. The suite profile artifact, pinned at four thousand four hundred and eighty-one tests, goes stale when a large block of tests disappears.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The guide's publication-cost evidence names the redo-record benchmark harness and its committed artifact.
- [hard] REQ-02: The journal-shaped benchmark script stops shipping, and contracts reference it nowhere.
- [hard] REQ-03: The per-test cost attribution table names only tests that exist.
- [hard] REQ-04: The build-budget note states figures re-derived after the change, holding or tightening.
- [hard] REQ-05: The suite-timing evidence artifact is refreshed, or its staleness is recorded with the test count it was pinned at and the condition for refreshing it.
- [hard] REQ-06: The guide's description of a storage round trip states the redo record.
- [hard] REQ-07: The change removes more lines than it adds.

planning.outcome: The testing guide names the redo-record harness as its publication-cost evidence.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One guide section plus the retired script and artifacts it cites as evidence.

title: Redo record foundation
description:
One redo record type, one way to write it durably, one way to apply it on either storage backend, and one proof of its crash behaviour, all reachable without changing how a mutation commits.

## Background

The redo record is the commit point that replaces a journaled rollback kernel. Before any publisher moves onto it, the mechanism has to exist whole: a vocabulary of put, delete, and event-append operations over data-root and worktree paths; a synced write that makes the record durable before any live file changes; an application that is idempotent under repetition; and a scoped comparison that refuses a mutation whose write targets moved underneath it.

The work in this phase adds the mechanism beside the one in use. Nothing in it changes how a mutation publishes, so the repository behaves exactly as it did while the mechanism is built and proven, and no adopter document goes stale. The storage layer declares its backends publicly, which is what lets a module land before its first caller under a build that denies warnings.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The workspace holds one redo record type, one writer, and one application routine per storage backend, with no second type or parallel entry point expressing the same thing.
- [hard] REQ-02: The record's crash matrix is proven in one suite over one point enum, and no second suite in the workspace proves it.
- [hard] REQ-03: The mechanism is unreachable from any publisher: no command, and no mutation session, commits through the record yet, and the repository's observable publication behaviour is unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-04: The workspace builds warning-free with the mechanism uncalled, through the storage layer's declared visibility rather than through a dead-code allowance.
- [hard] REQ-05: Each new module's rustdoc states its contract in at most one short paragraph of orientation, and none restates the retired kernel's protocol prose.
- [hard] REQ-06: The phase's additions stay within the per-task line ceilings its children state, and the total added is under 1,500 lines of production code.

planning.outcome: The record mechanism exists whole and proven, with no publisher on it yet.

title: Record publication cutover
description:
Every repository mutation commits through the redo record, the journaled kernel is gone, and the adopter documentation describes what the repository now does.

## Background

Repository publishers converge on one seam: the mutation session's apply. Moving the commit mechanism beneath that seam switches every repository publisher in one step.

Three things happen around it. Coverage that asserts the superseded rollback guarantee, and failure injection that names the kernel's points, are repointed or retired first, so each step compiles and passes. Creating an absent data root cannot use the record, because the record's home is inside the root that does not exist yet, so initialization gets a small publisher of its own and the scratch directory it creates carries an ignore entry composed from the repository's declarations. Initialization is also the kernel's last caller, so the kernel retires inside this phase: the interval where it sits unreferenced is one task long, spanned by a named dead-code allowance that the retiring task removes.

The adopter pages describing publication, recovery, the data-root layout, and the safe handling of that directory change here: a backup recipe that archives the whole data root starts capturing a pending commit point the moment the seam moves.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every repository mutation in the workspace commits through one redo record, and the creation of an absent data root is the only other path that writes repository state.
- [hard] REQ-02: The phase's diff across `crates/jit/src/commands/` changes no publisher's invocation of the mutation session, and every command family that published before the phase publishes after it.
- [hard] REQ-03: Publication convergence is proven in one place: the record's own conformance suite, with each publication consumer holding at most one test that it reaches the mechanism.
- [hard] REQ-04: The workspace contains no publication-failure injection that no longer fires, across the command layer, the storage suite, and the integration suites.
- [hard] REQ-05: The adopter documentation surface describes publication and recovery as the repository now performs them: no page instructs an operation that would remove or archive a pending commit point, and no page or declared gate scope names a journaled mechanism as live.
- [hard] REQ-06: No commit path the record replaced survives in the workspace, and the suite holds no test asserting a guarantee the record does not provide.
- [hard] REQ-07: No dead-code allowance introduced during the phase survives it, and the workspace builds with no warnings at each delivered child.
- [hard] REQ-08: Each delivered child leaves the suite passing with no test held out of the default run.

planning.outcome: Mutations commit through the record, the kernel is gone, and the adopter surface is in step.

title: Superseded design retirement
description:
The phased capture, the listing fingerprints, the mutation document closure, the plan hash, the transaction fields in command output, and the whole-file event-log rewrite are gone, with every declaration and document that named the old design restated.

## Background

The governing decision names ten constructs that go. Five of them — the rollback kernel, transaction backups, the staging directory, reverse actions, and worktree companions — leave with the kernel in the preceding phase. The five that remain are the apply-time revalidation of the whole read set, the plan hash over captured entries, the phased capture, the listing fingerprints, and the mutation document closure. Five of the ten name no construct under the name the criterion uses, so the check runs over a construct map rather than over a name search, and it runs here because only now is the whole set gone.

Two costs scaled with project history, and both fall here. Capture read and hashed the repository across six rounds; it becomes one round in the attempt and one in the preflight. The event log was rewritten whole on every mutation; the finalizer now emits the change as an offset with its bytes.

This is also where the repository's own declarations stop describing the old design. The invariant statements on atomic writes and derived-state coherence hold until the positioned append and the single-pass capture land. The contributor-facing architecture note and the Rust prose describing the retired machinery become false at the same moment, and the generated references follow their sources.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Each of the ten constructs the governing decision names is absent from the workspace, checked against the construct map in the planning investigation rather than by a name search, and the completion evidence records the check construct by construct.
- [hard] REQ-02: Creating an absent data root is the one publication path beside the redo record, named as an exception in a source guard that fails when a third appears.
- [hard] REQ-03: No declaration, generated projection, command output, command schema, or generated bridge definition in the repository names a retired mechanism.
- [hard] REQ-04: The contributor-facing material and the Rust prose describe one mechanism, and a reader following the architecture note's reading order reaches files that exist.
- [hard] REQ-05: The workspace builds with no warnings, the suite passes with no test held out of the default run, and the integration-test target count is within its budget.
- [hard] REQ-06: The phase's net effect on the workspace's Rust sources removes more lines than it adds, measured over its delivered children.

planning.outcome: The phased capture, the plan hash, and the whole-log rewrite are gone.

title: Mutation cost evidence
description:
A committed artifact shows that a mutation's wall time is bounded by what it changes, and the repository's testing guide cites evidence that exists.

## Background

The point of the mechanism change is a cost that stops scaling with project history. Two terms carried that scaling, and both are gone by the time this phase runs: the event log rewritten whole on every mutation, and the repository re-read and re-hashed across six capture rounds.

Protection is evidence, not a timing assertion. A wall-clock assertion would be the workspace's first throughput assertion, and the project's position is that elapsed time is the wrong thing to decide a test on. The evidence is a harness run over two builds, including a fixture whose event log is ten times larger with the issue set unchanged, so the log term is isolated from the issue-count term. The guide that cites publication-cost evidence is pinned today to an artifact produced by a harness built around the journal, so it moves to the new artifact in the same phase.

The phase edits the contributor material under `dev/` and `scripts/` and no page of the adopter surface, so the mechanical documentation gate, whose footprint is `docs/`, has nothing to check here.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: Every quantitative claim in the committed artifact traces to the committed harness, which reproduces it from the stated inputs.
- [hard] REQ-02: The repository's testing guide and benchmark contracts cite only evidence artifacts that exist, produced by harnesses that ship.
- [hard] REQ-03: The suite holds no wall-clock throughput assertion, and no test is held out of the default run to keep one quiet.
- [hard] REQ-04: The epic's cumulative Rust line balance from its base revision removes more lines than it adds, recorded in the artifact.

planning.outcome: Committed evidence shows a mutation's wall time bounded by what it changes.
